lesson_title: The Crowd That Never Changes: Chemical Equilibrium
hook_text: The shop looks frozen from outside. Inside, the doors have not stopped for a second.
clip_script: Stand outside the busiest shop in the centre and count the crowd through the glass: one hundred and fifty people. Come back fifteen minutes later: one hundred and fifty. Dead shop? Walk closer. Thirty people are pouring IN every minute — and thirty are pouring OUT. The count is frozen; the doors never stop. That is a chemical equilibrium: forward reaction in the front door, reverse reaction out the back, and when the two rates match, the concentrations lock — while molecules keep converting in both directions every instant. Anyone who says the reaction stopped is counting heads through the window. Now push the system and watch it push back. Dump in extra reactant, and it leans away, consuming your addition. Heat it, and it leans toward the direction that soaks up heat. Squeeze it, and the gases flee to the side with fewer molecules. Every push is answered — but only partly. The see-saw settles tilted, never back where it started. And through all of it, one referee keeps score: K c, products over reactants. Add chemicals, squeeze, stir in catalyst — the score never moves. Only temperature can rewrite it. A frozen crowd, a stubborn see-saw, and a referee loyal to one thing.
visual_style: Time-lapse of a shopfront with a fixed crowd counter while doors blur with motion; cut to a cartoon see-saw absorbing dropped weights and settling at new tilts; a glowing scoreboard labelled Kc that shrugs off everything except a thermometer.
mood: Cool and hypnotic, with a stubborn-machine punchline.
pacing: Slow frozen-count reveal, quick-cut push-and-lean sequence, deadpan close on the unmovable scoreboard.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to push a system that always pushes back.
